Why retrofit programmes stall in year two

By Ada Fenwick, Head of Plant Engineering · 11 February 2026

Every retrofit programme we have audited began with a strong first year. Lines were converted, the maintenance backlog fell, and the business case looked exactly as it had been written. The second year is where the pattern breaks, and it breaks for a reason that has nothing to do with the equipment.

In year one a programme converts the lines that were already understood. The engineers who built them are still on site, the drawings match the plant, and the failure modes are the ones everybody has been complaining about for a decade. In year two the programme reaches the lines nobody has opened since commissioning.

The documentation gap is the real constraint

Across nineteen plants, the median time to convert a line rose from nine days in year one to twenty-six days in year two. Almost none of that increase was installation work. It was rediscovery: tracing loops that no drawing shows, and confirming interlocks that exist only in the memory of a shift supervisor who has since retired.

The teams that held their year-one pace did one thing differently. They treated documentation as a deliverable of every conversion rather than a task to be done at the end of the programme, and they paid for it out of the conversion budget rather than the engineering overhead.

We stopped counting converted lines and started counting lines we could hand to a new engineer without a tour.

— Operations director, food and beverage, Midlands

What to change before year two

  1. Convert one undocumented line early, on purpose, and measure it honestly.
  2. Fund the rediscovery work in the conversion budget, not the overhead.
  3. Make the as-built drawing the acceptance criterion for the line, not the commissioning sheet.

None of this is new advice. What is new is the size of the penalty for ignoring it: a programme that loses its pace in year two rarely recovers it in year three, because by then the people who understood year one have moved on. Our privacy policy prevents us naming the plants in this study, but the pattern held in every one of them.
